The real problem is that Twitter has shown that the verified status is up to moderation fiat. Say, if you invest money in it and you can get it revoked regardless based on a whim. I think with this action Twitter has shot itself in the foot in the long run when corporations and PR agencies realize that Twitter plays fast and loose with its own rules. Why would they want to advertise on a site that has been prooven to take their credibility away with the press off a button?

What was done wasn't the censorship, WHY it was done was. It was a frivolous action taken against an apparent opponent for something they ostensibly said that offended... someone. Threat of additional action, combined with an actual slightly threatening one is equivalent to a shot across the bow. Twitter said 'shut up'.

The thing that makes this about free speech in general is the demonstration that the purveyors of our speech (the ones who hold it in their databases and let others even see it) have a bias and a willingness to disrupt it (by disrupting you) through any means, even one almost obscenely unrelated and unconscionable.

I find it baffling that a mechanism to prove your identity would be subject to any kind of weaponization other than withholding it in the first place. How delegitimatizing is it for Twitter to say that they can revoke verification of someone's identity when they and everyone know full well that the identity is not in question? By smacking a user to essentially 'anon' status how does that help us even in knowing he is the bad actor if we are his opponents? Aren't they providing cover for bad activity (on the face)? This makes it clear (to me) that the verification checkmark is merely a paid badge, and Twitter aren't worthy to be paid for it.
